content:
Twice the Quran speaks of "the scriptures of Abraham and Moses" (87:19; 53:36–37). The Wikipedia article "Scrolls of Abraham" reports that most Muslim scholars take this as a reference to a lost scripture, and then sets out three candidates for what the scrolls "really" were.

One is the scripture of the Sabians, as J. M. Rodwell reported from the Fihrist. The second is the Jewish book of creation called the Sefer Yetzirah, and the third the apocryphal Testament of Abraham.

Each candidate implies that the Quran's scrolls can be traced to a known human book. This article aims to provide context to those identifications, insha'Allah, in seven answers: what the Quran says the scrolls contained, what Muslims claim about them, and what the Fihrist, the Sefer Yetzirah and the Testament of Abraham turn out to be when each is read.

The Quran places Abraham among the prophets who received revelation: "And we revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants" (4:163).[1]

The Quran describes the scrolls by their teaching alone. Surah 87 ends: "He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself And mentions the name of his Lord and prays. But you prefer the worldly life, While the Hereafter is better and more enduring. Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, The scriptures of Abraham and Moses" (87:14–19).[1]

Al-Ṭabarī records the early commentators' views on what "this" refers to, and judges that it means the verses just before it: success through purification, remembrance of God and prayer, and the Hereafter preferred to this world.[2] Ibn Kathīr calls this "a good, strong choice", and cites a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Bazzār, that when these verses were revealed the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "All of this was in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."[3]

Surah 53 gives a longer list. It asks whether a man "has not been informed of what was in the scriptures of Moses And [of] Abraham, who fulfilled [his obligations] - That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives And that his effort is going to be seen - Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense And that to your Lord is the finality" (53:36–42).[1] Ibn Kathīr introduces the verses that follow as God's own account: "Then He began to explain what He had revealed in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."[4]

Muslims believe that God revealed scripture to Abraham, and they make no claim that it survives. The believer's creed in the Quran names it: "We have believed in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob" (2:136).[1]

Al-Qurṭubī adds a point of method. The verse, he writes, "did not mean that these words themselves are in those scrolls; it is the meaning, that is, the meaning of this speech is found in those scrolls".[5] The Quran claims a shared teaching, and it makes no claim to quote a text.

Later reports tried to say more. The long report of Abū Dharr, recorded by al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr, says that God revealed a hundred and four books, ten scrolls of them to Abraham, and that his scrolls were parables, beginning: "O king, given power, tested and deluded, I did not send you to heap up the world, but to turn away from Me the prayer of the oppressed".[5][6]

Ibn Kathīr notes that Ibn Ḥibbān judged the report sound, while Ibn al-Jawzī listed it among fabricated reports and blamed its narrator, Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām.[6] Al-Ṭabarī preserves a simpler report from Abū al-Jald, that the scrolls of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramaḍān, before the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Quran.[2]

The test for any proposed identification is therefore the content the Quran gives. A candidate book that teaches purification, prayer, the priority of the Hereafter, individual responsibility and recompense for one's own striving fits the description. A book that teaches something else does not.

Rodwell, in the preface to his translation of 1861, wrote that according to the Fihrist, as read by Aloys Sprenger, the Ḥanīfs were called "Sabeites" and "said to have received the Volumes (Sohof) or Books of Abraham". He added that from these books "Muhammad derived the legends of Ad and Themoud".[7]

The Fihrist tells a different story. Ibn al-Nadīm says he read it "in an old book" that seemed to come from the library of the caliph al-Maʾmūn, and he remarks that "most of the Ḥashwiyya and the common people believe it".

The book was by Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, a client of the caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd. He said he had translated it "from the book of the Ḥanafāʾ, who are the Abrahamic Sabians, who believed in Abraham and carried from him the scrolls that God sent down to him".[8]

The same translator adds that he inserted "the proofs needed from the Quran and from the reports that came from the Messenger", and from converts such as Kaʿb al-Aḥbār and Wahb ibn Munabbih.[8] His book is an Abbasid compilation of the ninth century, two hundred years after the Quran, and it draws on the Quran itself. It cannot have been the Prophet's source, and Ibn al-Nadīm himself signals his doubt about it.

The translator's own figures show which way the borrowing ran. His book counts a hundred and four revealed books, ten scrolls of them for Abraham and ten for Moses before the Torah, among 124,000 prophets.[8]

Those are the figures of the Muslim report of Abū Dharr.[6] An Abbasid book that repeats a Muslim hadith tells us what Muslims of the ninth century were reading, and nothing about a source older than the Quran.

The Sefer Yetzirah, the "Book of Creation", describes how God created the world through "32 secret paths of wisdom": the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet and ten sefirot, or numbers.[9] Its closing paragraph tells how "our father Abraham" contemplated these mysteries and how God made a covenant with him. On the strength of that paragraph, later Jewish tradition named Abraham as its author.[9][10]

The Jewish Encyclopedia article that Wikipedia cites for this identification says exactly that, and dates "the essential elements of the book" to the third or fourth century. Sefaria's summary of current scholarship puts it between the third and sixth centuries.[9][10] The Jewish Encyclopedia article says nothing about the Quran.

The Sefer Yetzirah teaches a cosmology of letters and numbers. It contains none of the content the Quran gives for the scrolls: nothing on the Hereafter being better than this world, on one soul not bearing another's burden, or on recompense for one's own striving. On the Quran's own test, it is a different book.

The Testament of Abraham is an apocryphal story in which Abraham, near death, is taken on a tour of heaven and watches souls being judged. M. R. James, who first edited its Greek text in 1892, concluded that it was "originally put together in the second century by a Jewish Christian", probably in Egypt.[11]

In its longer form, Abraham watches the trial of a soul whose good and evil deeds weigh exactly equal. James summarises the outcome: "Ultimately, owing to the intercession of Abraham, the soul in question gains eternal life".[11] The soul's fate is settled by another person's prayer.

The scrolls of Abraham, as the Quran describes them, teach the reverse: "no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives" (53:38–39).[1] Ibn ʿAbbās, as al-Ṭabarī records, explained that before Abraham a man would be punished for his kinsman's deed, until Abraham conveyed that no one is held to account for another's sin.[12] A book whose central scene turns on intercession cannot be the source of a teaching that rules it out.

Wikipedia supports the Testament of Abraham identification with a single reference: the "Tafsir and Commentary on 87: 18-19 & 53: 36-37" of Abdullah Yusuf Ali and Muhammad Asad.[13] That reference is to the notes of two twentieth-century translators of the Quran, and it offers no study of the Testament's text.

When the comparison is made, the result is the same for every candidate. The Fihrist's book post-dates the Quran and quotes it, the Sefer Yetzirah is about letters and numbers, and the Testament contradicts 53:38. None of them contains the teaching the Quran attributes to the scrolls.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) gave Muslims a rule for reports from earlier scriptures that cannot be checked: "Do not believe the people of the Scripture or disbelieve them, but say: 'We believe in Allah and what is revealed to us'".[14] The Quran's description of the scrolls is what Muslims hold to, and no later book is needed to confirm it.

A writer copying from a book would have reason to name a book his hearers could find. The Quran names one that, by its own account, they could not, and it gives its teaching in a few lines. The appeal works only as a claim of continuity: what Muḥammad brings is "in the former scriptures", taught to Abraham and Moses before him (87:18–19).[1]

That claim runs through the Quran's account of Abraham. "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was one inclining toward truth, a Muslim [submitting to Allah]" (3:67), and the Prophet was told "to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth" (16:123).[1]

Ismail al-Faruqi read Judaism, Christianity and Islam as successive moments of one Abrahamic religious consciousness, faulting the earlier two in their historical texts and honouring the revelation behind them.[15] We set out the Quran's account of Abraham's family in our article on Ishmael in the Quran and Genesis.

The verses that follow the list in surah 53 recall that God "destroyed the first [people of] 'Aad And Thamud" and the people of Noah (53:50–52).[1] Rodwell took those names as proof of a borrowed book. The Quran says of those peoples that "No one knows them but Allah" (14:9), and it tells their stories in its own words throughout.[1]

The bottom line

The Quran describes the scrolls of Abraham by their teaching: purification and prayer, the Hereafter above this world, no soul bearing another's burden, and full recompense for one's own striving. Muslims believe that scripture was revealed and lost, and they say so plainly.

The three proposed sources fail when they are read. The Fihrist's "Sabian" book is a ninth-century compilation that inserts the Quran's own proofs.

The Sefer Yetzirah is a later Jewish book about letters and numbers. The second-century Testament of Abraham saves a soul through Abraham's intercession, which is the teaching 53:38 denies.

The scrolls, as the Quran presents them, are known only through the Quran's summary, and that summary matches none of the books offered in their place. God knows best.

  3. Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, ed. Sāmī ibn Muḥammad Salāma (Riyadh: Dār Ṭayba, 1999), vol. 8, pp. 382–383, on 87:18–19, https://shamela.ws/book/8473/4428.
  4. Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, vol. 7, p. 465, on 53:37–38, https://shamela.ws/book/8473/3963.

  12. Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, vol. 22, pp. 542–543, on 53:37, report of ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās, https://shamela.ws/book/43/13172.
  13. Wikipedia, "Scrolls of Abraham", the section "Identification" and its references, as read on 23 November 2026.
  14. Sahih al-Bukhari 4485, report of Abū Hurayra.
  15. Al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life (International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2nd edition, 1992), chapter 2, section II.
